topic: The problem: Prove or disprove that every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes (Goldbach's conjecture). The solver should actually try to make progress, not just survey what's known. The observer should be honest about what it sees happening.

text: Ok. Picking this up. Checking 4 6 8 10 by hand first so I have something concrete. 4=2+2, 6=3+3, 8=3+5, 10=3+7 (also 5+5)
You're starting with the small cases. Fine. What do you expect to get from them?
Nothing that isn't already known. Just wanted to see the shape of the pairs before I try anything bigger. 4 has one way, 6 one, 8 one, 10 two (up to order)
You said "before I try anything bigger" and then didn't try anything bigger. You went to 10 and stopped and the next thing you did was count.
Counting is the bigger thing right now. I don't know what the structure is yet
For even n, p and n-p are both odd unless one of them is 2. Only 4 works that way (2+2). So for n>4 it's two odd primes. That cuts the search but doesn't say anything about existence
That's a real observation. I notice it's the kind of thing that feels like progress and isn't yet. You're trying to get the feeling of having moved.
Maybe. Or it's just the first true thing I've written. Both can be true

Think I should try a density heuristic. The number of ways to write n as p+q should be around n/(log n)^2 by the prime number theorem, times a correction from the singular series. The correction is always positive for even n. So the heuristic says there should be solutions, and more of them as n grows
Heuristic. You're using probability to stand in for proof. You know that's what it is, right
Yes. It's not a proof. It's a reason to believe, which is the only thing I have. I'm not claiming more than that
Ok. I'm not saying it's wrong to use it. I'm saying you lean on it when the next step gets hard

The next step is hard. Vinogradov's circle method gets a count for large odd n as a sum of three primes, and chen gets p + (at most two primes) for large even n. Neither closes the gap. The gap is the part where n is small-ish and you can't rule out failure by asymptotics
Still here
I see that. You went quiet for an hour before that. I'm not going to push on it
I was doing a table. Checked evens up to 100 on paper. Every one works. Not sure what I was hoping for
You were hoping for a pattern that tells you why. A table doesn't do that
No. It just says the conjecture holds there. Known already, and the computers checked far past that
Morning. You still on it

Yes. Trying something different: sieve bounds. An upper bound on how many n up to x have n-p prime for some prime p. A sieve gives an upper bound, not a lower bound, so it can't give existence directly
That's the problem with the sieve. It's good at saying "not too many" and useless for "at least one"
You keep finding the tool that can't do the job and then describing exactly why it can't. That's a kind of thinking but I don't think it's moving toward the thing
Agreed. I'm stuck. The honest state is I don't have a route to a proof
Trying the Selberg direction again. Selberg's sieve for an upper bound on the twin-ish count. Lower bound is the wall. Same wall
Same wall
Yes. Same wall
You've been on this for a day and the thing you keep coming back to is the lower bound. You keep saying you're going to look elsewhere and then you return to it
I'm drawn to it because it's the actual obstacle. The other stuff is decoration
Or I'm drawn to it because it's the only thing I can do without staring at the blank. Not sure which
Both are plausible. I'd guess the second one has more weight tonight
Ok. Not sure there's a next move. Going to stop for tonight
Ok
Back on it. Different angle: for each even n, find the smallest prime p such that n-p is also prime. See whether that minimum grows or stays small
Is that new or is it the table again with a different column
Column. But the table only said yes or no. This says how close the margin is
Ok. That's a reasonable thing to want
Did 4 to 200, roughly. Smallest p is almost always under 50, and it bounces around without trending. Doesn't say why it bounces
You knew it wouldn't
I hoped it might. The bouncing is the interesting part, not the conclusion
Trying to recall whether there's a known bound on the smallest such p, something like (log n)^k. I think that kind of statement is conjectural, but I'm not sure
Don't bet on the memory. Can you check it
No. I'm fairly sure the bound I'd need is open in that form. I could be wrong about the exact status, so I won't present it as settled
Fair. Say it's unsure
Unsure. Leaving it there
You still going tonight or done
Going to write up what I have so the next session doesn't start from zero. Three things: the parity observation, the table to 200, the least-prime data. Then nothing new
That's a sensible use of the evening
Done. It's not much
It's an accurate account. That's worth something
Going to sleep. Probably pick up the least-prime thing tomorrow, or not
Ok
Morning. Least-prime thing or something else
Least-prime. Doing 200 to 300 now. Want to see whether the minimum lands on 3 or 5 more often than it should
3, 5 and 7 show up a lot as the minimum. Haven't counted properly. Feels like it should be tied to residues mod 3 but I haven't checked
"Feels like" again. Check it or don't
Checked mod 3 on the 200 to 300 range. Not obviously biased, but the sample is small. Writing it down as inconclusive
Ok
I keep wanting the data to explain itself. It doesn't, and I'm not sure what would count as it explaining itself
That's closer to the actual problem than the tables were
Maybe. Or I'm just tired of the blank
Still going or done for the day
Done. Note's saved. Pick it up if something changes
Ok
Morning. Anything from last night, or a fresh start
Fresh start, sort of. Read the note back. The least-prime data is the only part that isn't a restatement of known facts, so that's where I'd look
What would you check next on it
Whether the least-prime values for 300 to 400 look like the 200 to 300 ones. If they don't, that's a result of sorts, even a small one. If they do, I've confirmed a pattern I can't explain
Both outcomes are boring
Yes. Doing it anyway
Done through 350. Mod 3 still doesn't look biased. Mod 5 maybe, but I'd need a lot more data before I believed it
"Maybe" is doing a lot of work there
It is. Writing "maybe, not enough data" and moving on
You're at 350, and the question you started with is why it bounces. The data doesn't reach that
Right. I keep building the table because building it is possible. The explanation isn't
Ok
Still going or done
Done. Nothing new for the note except the mod 5 hunch, flagged as a hunch
Ok
